The rapid spread of COVID-19 in China was accompanied by intense speculation and misinformation in China's social media environment. This study examines the evolution of two widespread online rumors during this period and identifies the factors that contributed to their dissemination. By combining network analysis, rumor diffusion theory, and psychological perspectives, our research reveals that the rumors' ability to spread was influenced by their alignment with common sense, the credibility of the sources spreading them, and the emotional resonance they had with users. We found that rumors that originated from authoritative sources were able to spread more widely, despite losing none of their credibility in users' eyes, even after they were debunked. Furthermore, we found that the engagement users had with these rumors, whether emotionally or intellectually, did not decrease after they were proven to be false. This has significant implications for online misinformation in China and elsewhere, given the critical role that credibility and psychological connection play in the continued spread of rumors even after they are disproven.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been developed by combining deep imaging and spectroscopy of planetary nebulae. This method leverages the distinct P-NVE features in spectroscopy and bulge-like P-NVE populations in imaging, allowing for accurate distance estimates despite some data limitations. Applying this technique to early Fornax3D data within the Fornax cluster, a reliable distance module was established with results consistent with established measurements for this area. A refined analysis using only galaxies with extensive P-NVE data and high stellar mass in the cluster's center yielded a mean distance of 18.89 megaparsecs with a margin of error of 0.57 megaparsecs. This result is also in line with other distance measurements for this area.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity in their design. To address the limitations of existing data processing systems, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance on real-world datasets from various sources, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and relational databases by orders of magnitude.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in six-dimensional Euclidean space.

Requiring accurate classification is a fundamental requirement in various deep learning applications. Despite achieving outstanding performance in various tasks, such as image recognition, video analysis and speech processing, neural networks still struggle with sensitive and rare classifications. Loss function modification has been an effective strategy in enhancing classification performance but the underlying reasons behind this approach are not well understood. This work uses decision boundary visualization and risk estimation as ongoing projects in the deep learning laboratory, to investigate the link between loss function, classification accuracy and decision boundary behavior. We demonstrate that modifying the loss function is equivalent to adjusting the confidence of the network in its predictions and this confidence affects the classification performance at the edge of the training dataset. Furthermore, we observe that the shape of the decision boundary varies with the choice of loss function and this affects the classification performance at extreme data points. To validate these findings, we conducted an experiment using the MNIST dataset and our results showed that networks with high confidence in their predictions tend to achieve better performance in rare classification than those with low confidence.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be simulated effectively to capture its microstructural development properly. It has been observed that polymer crystallization models based on the degree of crystallinity are insufficient for predicting its mechanical behavior, given that crystal size and orientation also significantly influence this behavior. In order to accurately simulate the thermomechanical properties of polymers, a new model has been developed that incorporates the influence of temperature, deformation rates, and strain-induced crystallization on polymer microstructure. This model has been applied to simulate the non-isothermal uniaxial extension of a specific polymer material, with the resulting simulations showing good agreement with actual experimental data on the development of crystallinity, orientation, and temperature throughout the deformation process.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

Continuous phase modulation techniques offer reliable data transmission through Doppler shift compensation, which is critical in applications with substantial motion.  This paper presents an innovative threshold-based delay-enhancement method for traditional non-coherent differential detection of CPM signals.  By analyzing the detected signal's behavior, a proposed delay strategy aims to minimize false dissolution of continuous phase trajectories, thereby reducing the desired differential signal's error threshold.  Compared to the standard practice of adjusting the threshold in proportion to the signal-to-noise ratio, the proposed method's simulations demonstrate a 50% average reduction in threshold values, resulting in a 33% average decrease in required code diversity and enabling support for up to 30% higher maximum delay values.  The proposed method's effectiveness is further demonstrated through simulations of motion-induced delay in outdoor millimeter-wave communications.

A previously proposed quantum theory predicts that spacetime must possess a minimum level of compressibility to prevent the formation of singularities. This requirement is more stringent than the Einstein field equations' necessity for vanishing compressibility, as it derives compressibility from the curvature term in Einstein's equation. By treating Einstein's gravity as a phenomenological model, we demonstrate that the capability can be understood through the compressibility of geometric fluctuations. It is shown that the minimum compressibility standard can only be met if the geometric fluctuations are negative, implying that the compressibility is a complex quantity. Consequently, this standard is not met within the framework of general relativity. Nevertheless, we display that the capability can be achieved when the Einstein field equations are modified to include a cosmological constant, specifically in the case of an FRW cosmology.

Humans employ if-then reasoning to make inferences based on general knowledge. Despite significant progress in AI, achieving this same level of reasoning on massive data sets has proven challenging. We have created ATOMIC, a vast knowledge base comprising 137,000 sentences with explicit if-then structures, allowing for various types of conclusions to be drawn from premises. This atlas of machine common knowledge opens doors to investigating intricate aspects of reasoning and, as demonstrated in our studies, yields substantial gains in tasks like reasoning-based evaluation and natural language generation.

Quantum linear algebra applications are significantly enhanced through the HHL algorithm, despite its overall high computational requirements. Although HHL outperforms classical methods for large-scale systems in need of extensive matrix inversions, its dependence on intricate quantum components like Fourier transforms and binary arithmetic hinders its effectiveness on near-term, fault-tolerant quantum devices. In our investigation, we focused on optimizing the HHL algorithm for these devices and applied it to solve complex problems involving chemical reactivity, as demonstrated by a bond-breaking case involving hydrogen molecules.

To enhance multi-modal training for deep learning-based speech recognition systems, it's essential to incorporate text data into the training process. However, utilizing both speech and text data in models leads to an imbalance where the stronger data source dominates the model's learning. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in models that combine both data sources, causing them to become biased towards either speech or text, depending on which data source is more prevalent. To address this challenge, a novel technique is developed which employs a bidirectional attention mechanism to counteract this effect and maintain a balance between the data sources. Furthermore, to prevent the model from becoming entirely dependent on either data source, a strategy is proposed to alternate the frequency with which speech and text data are used in the model's training. Experimental evaluations conducted on the Librispeech corpus demonstrate a significant improvement in speech recognition accuracy, outperforming current state-of-the-art results.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of the set of uniform parking functions for growing integers n. We define a natural metric $\delta_n$ to gauge the set of uniform parking functions at n, and our main findings include:
1. To define a meaningful limit as n approaches infinity, the metric $\delta_n$ must be scaled by a factor of n. This gives us a rescaled metric $\Delta_n$, and we prove that as n grows, the set of uniform parking functions at n, when measured by $\Delta_n$, converges to a circle with a radius of 1.
2. An alternative analysis using combinatorial techniques confirms our asymptotic result.
3. We also examine the set of uniform parking functions at n for growing integers n in a more general form, and identify conditions under which we can guarantee the set's asymptotic behavior is similar to that of standard parking functions.
4. One such condition is that n must be prime, and in this case, we find that the set of uniform parking functions at n is identical to the set of standard parking functions at n.
5. Another condition is provided by a formula of Knop, which enables us to determine the asymptotic behavior of the set of uniform parking functions at n for growing integers n, and especially enables us to establish that the set's asymptotic character is always that of a sphere with a radius of 1.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking supercurrent. The adjustment of gate voltage can modify the conductivity of these nanowires without affecting their temperature or current characteristics. The data show that quantum phase slips are unlikely unless the nanowires are very short, specifically less than 20 nm, or if there is gate-controlled Coulomb obstruction, which we determine could result from the accumulation of charge or magnetic field-induced localization. The movement of blockades along the conduction diagram suggests that the nanowires have variable lengths, confirming the effectiveness of Coulomb obstruction as a explanation. Moreover, the behavior of long nanowires under microwave radiation resembles the Coulomb blockade scenario. The movement of blockades can be eliminated by incorporating oxygen into the nanowires, a process that affects the electron-mean-free-path rather than the average length. This investigation highlights the potential for controlling DC and AC conductivity through the localization of electrons in nanoscales without evidence of coherent quantum phase slips.

In innovative view video forecasting, a model is desired that can accurately predict non-euclidean view video frames from limited historical information. To achieve this, a novel dual-latent representation technique is proposed, featuring two latent spaces to capture both visual characteristics and view-specific information. The model employs a dual-learning approach to effectively connect the two latent spaces and outputs the predicted view video frames. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the proposed method to outperform existing alternatives in various view-changing scenarios.

In this research, inter-orbital interaction was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables the creation of complex quantum systems for realizing quantitative metrics of wave function overlap, phase structure, and inter-particle interaction. Specifically, we generated two types of oxygen vacancy orbitals in titanium dioxide that interact through superexchange interaction, and our results showed that in addition to having a significant spin gap, this system also exhibits a cycloidal phase characterized by a non-trivial topological phase structure as a result of an all-optical effect.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied theoretically. Using a constituent quark model with relativistic effects, we calculated the masses and radiative transition probabilities between states of the Ω-baryon. Compared to experimental values, discrepancies in calculated masses ranged from 0.2 to 0.5 GeV, with the inclusion of a quark gluon interaction leading to improved mass estimates. Nevertheless, the primary source of this divergence remained uncertain. By comparing calculated and experimental transition probabilities, we identified potential markers of quark formation and matter density within the Ω-baryon.

Understanding the behavior of respiratory viruses within closed environments is crucial for developing effective prevention strategies. To gain insight into this phenomenon, we examine the spread of a infectious agent on an urban bus using a mathematical model. We validate a well-established model, which assumes the viral particles mix instantly, by comparing its predictions to data from controlled respiratory virus experiments. Our analysis shows that this model accurately predicts the evolution of infection within the bus, even when incorporating variables such as airflow. To further illustrate the model's usefulness, we demonstrate its ability to simulate scenarios involving various prevention measures.

Researchers explored the effects of spin-orbit proximity coupling in nanoscale materials, examining the behavior of spin-orbit moments in magnetic multilayers. A theoretical model, incorporating spin-orbit proximity coupling and surface roughness, was applied to bi-layer structures comprising cobalt and bismuth. Calculations demonstrated that spin-orbit proximity coupling and surface roughness both contribute to the dispersion of spin-orbit moments within the multilayer layers. However, surface roughness was found to dominate the behavior, while coupling showed a weaker influence on the spin-orbit moments' spectrum. Experimentally obtained imaging and spectroscopy data from a specific Bi/Co sample are compared to theoretical predictions, showcasing good agreement and further supporting the key role of surface roughness in spin-orbit behavior. Additionally, this research highlights the significance of considering interface roughness in predictions of spin-orbit effects for various materials, including those with strong spin-orbit interaction.

This research tackles the time-invariant fractional Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space, with the aim of finding approximate solutions for a type of generalized Mie-like potential that includes an fractional derivative. To this end, the fractional Schrödinger equation is replaced with a pseudo-differential equation, which can be solved for the potential's generalized Mie-like form. Subsequently, the paper presents the ground-state wave function and energy calculations for this potential, concluding that the approach yields accurate results near the origin and large distances, with a proposed generalization to include a variable power within the fractional derivative.

We analyze how enforcing a uniform weight variation serves to enhance the
predictive accuracy of neural networks by making them more adaptable to
Lipschitz regularization methods. We demonstrate that optimally configuring
the hyperparameters of weight regularization and Lipschitz restriction can
significantly boost the efficacy of neural networks in various applications.

We investigate the production of Drell-Yan diphoton and same-sign same-flavor dilepton pairs within the framework of third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models. These models, which combine lepton and quark properties in one particle, can explain certain discrepancies in particle physics data. We focus on the T-Quark gauge vector leptoquark, which interacts with quarks and leptons through the fundamental and symmetric doublet representation. We utilize the Monte Carlo event generator Sherpa to implement the calculation of these processes at the level of Leading Order Monte Carlo events, combined with Leading Log Precision for the Parton Shower, and evaluate their potential impact on the Weak Boson Scattering process and top quark pair production. We compare our results to existing studies, and recommend a set of customizable input parameters to facilitate further research.

Understanding the physics behind medical imaging is crucial for accurately interpreting and utilizing imaging data. Quantitative CT imaging, which provides numerical tissue information, and qualitative PET imaging, which provides visual tissue images, differ in this aspect due to different capture processes. To bridge this gap, we propose a multimodal learning framework that incorporates quantitative and qualitative imaging data while accounting for measurement uncertainties. This framework, designed to withstand out-of-distribution data, is utilized for low-dose PET image reconstruction. We leverage a trained model to predict high-dose PET images at intermediate doses, continuously adapting to new data through iterative re-training. To evaluate our method, we conducted experiments with actual clinical data from both PET and CT machines. Our results show that this framework can successfully reconstruct high-dose PET images from low-dose data with significant reductions in radiation exposure required for accurate diagnosis.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper delves into the connection between CT and a modern coreference resolution approach, examining whether features derived from CT enhance the ability of machines to resolve coreferences. Through a series of experiments, our findings indicate that, when using a fully trained model, features based on CT do not significantly improve coreference resolution performance. Nevertheless, we observed a promising effect when CT-derived features were used to train a model from scratch, leading to a slight increase in scores. Furthermore, a analysis of the data revealed that the relationship between CT centers and coreferential markers is not universally consistent, suggesting that the relationship between words and their referring expressions is inherently complex and influenced by various linguistic factors.

In order to further enhance wireless network security and prevent unauthorized access, accurate estimation of a device's physical location and range is a key functionality with significant implications for various applications including enterprise, military, and healthcare sectors. This range estimation task, also known as fingerprinting, involves linking a device's connection details to its associated distance from a designated access point. In recent years, various methods have been proposed to estimate this distance using different machine learning models, but these approaches have been largely unsupervised and unable to account for instances where a device operates at a extended range from the access point. In contrast, this research introduces an innovative technique for supervised range estimation where a device's connection to a prolonged range results in an inferred, rather than manually specified value. The proposed method involves training a professional AI model, specifically a neural network, using a unique, blended learning approach that combines three distinct training methods: conventional, hybrid, and anomaly-seeking techniques. When tested using a real WiFi network dataset, the research shows that the proposed technique accurately estimates both a device's physical location and range from an access point with a 24% and 15% reduction in error, respectively, compared to existing range estimation methods.

The Beam Disruption Instability (BDI) problem arises in Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs) due to the high-power beams interacting with the spent beam trapped in wheel magnets, and it poses a significant challenge for the development of future high-energy medical applications and multi-bunch operations. Since wheel magnets inevitably incorporate filling configurations that leave a portion of the beam orbit, a regenerative beam disruption instability has emerged as a key issue in designing and operating future ERLs. This paper examines various filling configurations that exhibit distinct levels of ring impedance, following the placement of wheel magnets within the ring. It is evident that filling configurations significantly affect the beam-trained feedback system's performance. Notably, configurations featuring front section wheel magnets exhibit improved stability performance compared to those located in the straight section, which is crucial for implementing beam feedback systems. Additionally, this analysis provides guidelines for optimizing filling configurations and reducing the effect of ring impedance. It is proposed that, in order to minimize the effect of ring impedance, wheel magnets should be placed closer to the start of each straight section in multi-bunch ERLs.

Using the dual-field-theory approach, we have implemented a 6-particle one-loop scattering amplitude calculation in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. The scattering amplitude was obtained in a general form that factors into three separate amplitudes, each representing the scattering of two gluons. This decomposition exposes the central-emission vertex, a fundamental component in the dual theory, which governs the emission of two gluons. Our analysis has yielded a precise expression for the central-emission vertex, a non-trivial result that demonstrates symmetry under the permutation of the two gluons. This key finding is particularly significant in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, given the inherent difficulty in identifying this vertex through traditional means due to the overwhelming number of possible six-gluon amplitudes.

The behavior of stretched polymers under force has been thoroughly examined in various configurations, yet there's a lack of analysis on shaped bristles with a large number of loops until now. Utilizing mesoscopic simulations of good solvents, we developed a strong understanding of bristle dynamics and identified subregions that are completely free from exclusion areas, confirming that shaped bristles also follow the $f \propto \chi^{-1}$ law when analyzing looped regions. A critical condition for loop formation was also determined and found to be directly linked to the specific shape of the bristle. A particular example of bristle models was then proposed, consisting of tethers connected to loops at their ends, which can transfer forces to loops through entanglements. This model bristle maintains its overall length even under stretching forces, demonstrating a distinctive power-law pattern when analyzing loop forces. This model can be distinguished from others like star-bristles that undergo significant contraction when stretched.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when its vertex set can be distinguished uniquely by a set of distances, using a metric dimension of h. However, for many graphs, especially those with a large number of vertices, this high dimensional requirement can significantly impede its potential applications. In response to this limitation, we introduce a new parameter, called the beta-dimensional space (βDS) or shortened metric dimension, to accommodate graphs that can function effectively with a lower dimensional space, albeit not fully identifiable. We examine betaDS properties, determine its relationship to the standard metric dimension, and discuss its potential in enhancing the functionality of a graph while minimizing its dimensional space.

We've created an intelligent system that automatically identifies variable sources from all-sky maps made from Fermi-LAT data, which collects radiation from the sky. This machine learning-based approach, built using 42 months of data and 39 known variable sources, prioritizes certain sources and flags uncertain ones for human review. The system's structure consists of eight filters that narrow down sources based on radiance patterns, followed by three machine learning models – Extreme Randomized Forests, Gradient Boosting, and Neural Networks – that identify variable sources. By comparing the system's output with actual variable sources and others that remain in the maps after removing artificial objects, we found that it recovers 96% of known variables and affects 13% of remaining sources, which it considers new and variable. When applying this system to all-sky maps, it finds 2600 to 3400 variable sources, depending on the sensitivity to radiation, which could be further validated with other data.

In over voting situations, the serial dictatorship mechanism yields an efficient and strategy-proof outcome by following a predetermined order of preference consideration. However, this approach can lead to inefficient results when users rank options by their own preference rather than a designated order. To rectify this issue, we propose a new approach, which we call the 'extended serial dictatorship', incorporating the users' original preferences while maintaining their underlying rank of consideration. This variant ensures social welfare maximization and retains strategy-proof properties, thereby preserving the beneficial characteristics of the original serial dictatorship for users in a defined ranking of consideration.

The number of small asteroids orbiting the sun has been recorded, but the number of binary asteroids has been estimated to be only about 100 out of an estimated 100,000 total asteroids in this category. To expand the scope of a previous binary asteroid investigation, a comprehensive search was conducted through archival images from the Pan-STARRS1 telescope, yielding approximately 1.4 million high-quality images spanning a 4.5 year period. A sophisticated detection method was developed to locate asteroids with two components in a single image, or a single component in two images showing the same asteroid. This approach resulted in the identification of 24 potential binary asteroids, in addition to 15 known binary asteroids found in previous studies, and 45 other asteroid shapes thought to be correct based on images, but without sufficient data to confirm this. The estimated total number of binary asteroids in the size range of 100 to 300 meters in diameter is likely around 200 to 300, but more evidence is needed to verify this finding.

This research addresses the parameters estimation challenge for a partially linear regression model where the mean response variable is influenced by a mean network exposure, using data from social networks. The model assumes that the effect of the network exposure is linear, whereas the impact of individual network members is nonlinear. To analyze this model, we employ a combination of influence function and semi-parametric efficient score, enabling parameters estimation through the plug-in method and central limit theorem for the estimated parameters. Furthermore, the research adapts the Bickel and Ritov (1999) theorem to guarantee the consistency of the non-parametric component estimation and provides a test statistic for testing the significance of network peer influences using the wild bootstrap method.

This study introduces novel Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative operators based on the Leibniz rule. It derives key properties, including product, quotient, and chain rules for these operators. Specifically, we establish the Leibniz rule for the new Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional derivative operator and its converse, demonstrating their equivalence. Furthermore, we prove the compatibility of the operator with the gamma function and derive its product, quotient, and chain rules. Our results are anticipated to facilitate research in mathematics, physics, and engineering, where fractional calculus is applied.

We introduce An AI Dungeon Master's Handbook, a groundbreaking, two-part challenge that requires separate solutions for two connected problems. Firstly, it calls for a method to train a dialogue system for one player, given a pre-existing group conversation, without relying on cost-prohibitive teacher data. Secondly, it demands a Theory-of-Mind-based model that can predict the focus and concerns of individual players within the group, incorporating reasoning about conflicting objectives. Both components are critical on their own, yet together they offer a distinctive and complex problem that reflects the underlying dynamics of Dungeons and Dragons. Our proposed approach addresses these challenges by separating the dialogue model from the Theory-of-Mind component and combining them in a hybrid that learns from player feedback alone. Through extensive experiments on extensive, real-world D&D data, our results show that An AI Dungeon Master's Handbook successfully interacts with players, surpassing human benchmarks by 5% in intent recognition and demonstrating superior performance in comparison to single-component models.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their bending capacities is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their complex geometries. This analysis uncovers the relationship between the spatial configurations of knotted proteins and their bending possibilities. Specifically, the study evaluates a broad range of protein knots, including trefoil and gutted varieties, to determine the relationship between their spatial arrangements and capacity for bending through a process known as slide permutation. This connection is represented by a precise mathematical formula that can be tested and refined with more data. Generally speaking, this research helps uncover the rules that govern the complex relationship between the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins and their bending capacities.

Let $\omega$ denote a symplectic form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that $\omega$ is non-degenerate, there exists an interval $(a,b)$ of positive numbers, including $1$, for which for every $c\in (a,b)$, there is a way to scale the form by $c$ and embed it via a map of degree $2$ into a blowup of $T^4$.

A detailed investigation of the conventional Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem reveals that the principle's validity depends on the type of symmetry being observed and whether it relates to a global or local symmetry. This analysis leads to the identification of four scenarios that violate the conventional NG theorem: three known cases involving a massless scalar field in both the global and local contexts, and the presence of a pseudoscalar Nambu-Goldstone mode in the local symmetry setting. A comprehensive study of these four cases analyzes their fundamental characteristics and the resulting theoretical frameworks. The study also delves into the specific mechanisms that lead to the violation of the conventional NG theorem, including the Higgs mechanism and its analogous effects in both the relativistic and nonrelativistic frameworks.

Recent studies on counterfactual language models focus on truth-filled counterfactuals, 
where models are trained to produce statements that are factually accurate. 
In contrast, phrasal counterfactuals, as observed in social media, often involve 
exchanging words or phrases to convey a different meaning or perspective. 
Although existing assessment methods evaluate counterfactuals with multiple correct answers, 
they do so using a single, often ambiguous example per task. In contrast, the following study assesses fluency and accuracy in tasks that include multiple counterfatural examples, varying in form and difficulty. Specifically, the study examines the performance of two advanced language models in producing high-quality phrasal counterfactuals. To accomplish this, the models are trained on a vast dataset of social media posts, incorporating nearly 13 million counterfactuals. The evaluation of the models is carried out through human-based assessments of counterfactuals generated in response to everyday sentences, in addition to customized evaluation tasks that involve altering specific words or phrases within structured contexts. The results show that both models successfully produce high-quality counterfactuals at a low cost, despite limitations in our design. The study also explores the implications of counterfactual generation for tasks such as paraphrasing, where models may over-rely on phrase exchanges, and summarization, where there is a notable lack of accuracy.

The epitaxial growth of thin films on substrates with misfit strain relief mechanisms offers a program for creating stress-free, crystalline materials with defined lattice parameters. While remote heteroepitaxy via graphene intermediaries has been effective for growing thin films on inert substrates like silicon or sapphire, there are limitations to its scalability due to the limited size of the graphene islands and their tendency to merge as the film grows. In this study, we investigated the epitaxial growth of Heusler films on graphene/sapphire using low-energy ion plating, and we found that the films could be divided into three categories based on the size of their islands under ultr-low supercritical substrate pre-treatment. By developing a compatible experimental technique, we were able to increase the film island size by raising the substrate slightly above the supercritical point. However, this caused the film islands to coalesce and switch to van der Waals epitaxy. By introducing a small amount of sulfur on the graphene, we were able to create a protective layer around the film islands and relieve the coalescence, allowing for larger film islands and expanding the remote heteroepitaxy regime. By simulating the results with a combination of first-principles calculations and kinetic Monte Carlo methods, we were able to understand the film island size distribution and strain relief mechanisms through the formation of grain boundaries or the exfoliation of film flakes from the surface. The development of sulfur-based protective films also enables the remote hetero

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the extended extended Frobenius code construction. This paper specifically investigates the class of $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes by determining their dimension. Additionally, we provide a detailed description of the null space of these codes, which includes a necessary and sufficient condition for another code to have $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linearity. This condition is met if the dual code can be successfully encoded using the extended extended Frobenius code construction.

Deep neural networks have had significant success in the area of classification, but many real-world tasks involve a more complex process where a network is trained on a single label that represents a set of relevant labels from a much larger database. This task is often referred to as instance-level labeling. In contrast to traditional multi-label classification, where all possible labels are considered equally important, instance-level labeling involves determining a subset of relevant labels from a large set, making it a more challenging problem. In this process, many valuable labels can be overlooked due to the limited nature of positive examples. In order to address this issue, we propose a novel way to augment positive labels by drawing additional examples from negative classes, effectively supplementing limited instance-level labeling data with multi-label examples. This approach is simple, cost-free, and can be applied to existing multi-label classification datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by incorporating it into a standard deep learning training process, and show that it leads to improved performance on a range of multi-label classification benchmarks.

Quantum systems can be described using mathematical tools from linear algebra and operator theory. A key framework for this purpose is the category of Hilbert spaces, which serves as a foundation for developing quantum theories. However, in the study of quantum systems, researchers often work with operators representing physical quantities and statuses of measurement outcomes, which can be mapped from Hilbert spaces to more abstract spaces. This process involves creating a pair of functors that map between the spaces of operators and statuses and the Hilbert spaces, respectively. In doing so, researchers preserve the underlying physical properties. A specific scenario involving the category of assemblies arises in the study of measurement outcomes, presenting a particular challenge. Despite this complication, a general framework exists that facilitates work with operator statuses while maintaining adherence to the physical principles, as embodied by the structure of assembly. The development of this idea is explored further in the paper's additional sections.

The exact mechanisms behind the emission of high-energy gamma-rays from nearby galaxies that exhibit bright radio signals, particularly giant radio galaxies, remain unclear. Two prominent models attempting to explain this phenomenon involve the accumulation of magnetic fields and extreme matter within these galaxies's dark matter halos, and the presence of accreting matter on supermassive black holes still in the early stages of growth. For the former model, it is anticipated that we should observe a connection between the emission of gamma-rays and the characteristics of magnetic fields in the accresembling disk systems. Utilizing broadband spectral data and magnetic field measurements from various giant radio galaxies, a study found that the emission of gamma-rays can be attributed to accresembling disk systems that undergo gamma-ray absorption, and it correlates with the strength of magnetic fields rather than other factors. As a result, the primary driver of high-energy gamma-rays in these galaxies are systems that accumulate magnetic fields and feature extremely low Compton ratios and complex spectral profiles.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and operator technique varying between recordings. This study aims to explore the impact of different noise levels and recording techniques on sound classification and proposes an method to address this issue. A feature extraction technique called Mel Frequency Band Power (MFBP) is compared to common techniques such as spectrogram-based, and it is found that MFBP-based classification performs better than conventional methods in various conditions. This observation motivates the use of a specific noise level and recording technique as an alternative to creating a massive training dataset. Furthermore, a model is proposed that is capable of handling varying noise levels and recording techniques by treating them as a single class, using a technique called one-class SVM to eliminate noise recordings. This model's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on publicly available datasets. The proposed method's performance is compared to conventional methods, and it is found that MFBP-based classification performs better than conventional methods in various conditions. The code for this project has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/HeartSoundClassification/ConvNet_with_Noise_Sep.

The proliferation of wearable devices for health monitoring has generated a vast amount of data, presenting a opportunity for machine learning-based analysis. However, data is being collected by multiple users on various devices across different locations, making it difficult to utilize a traditional centralized approach. In response, a new method called FedHealth is proposed for personalized classification on user data, drawing on the principles of federated learning and transfer learning. Within this framework, users participate in the training process by sharing local models, and a federated learning platform performs aggregating their contributions. The result is a capability to classify health data on a individual basis without requiring a central pool of data. Furthermore, FedHealth detects optimal participant contribution based on risk assessment, enabling secure operation in an uncertain environment. Experimental evaluations reveal significant improvements in accuracy when comparing FedHealth to standalone transfer learning on a large health dataset.

This study compares and contrasts the key elements of portfolio optimization strategies that go beyond the traditional mean-variance model. Some of the variants discussed involve improving the second moment estimation, adjusting for non-estimated risks, or employing alternative loss functions. The paper also explores connections between these methods and provides empirical evidence from a study on 25 stocks using historical data to test the theories.

The rising complexity of software systems, coupled with rapid technological advancements, has made it crucial to automate the process of understanding software, thereby freeing humans from mundane tasks, such as manually analyzing logs and tracking down bugs. This shift towards automation has sparked significant interest in retrieving and analyzing binary files, despite the difficulties posed by the low-level nature of this data. To address these challenges, a suite of advanced technologies including artificial neural networks, machine learning, and program analysis has been developed, providing a solid foundation for exploring binary files. In contrast to conventional binary analysis approaches, which focus on specific, narrow tasks, this community has adopted a broader perspective, emphasizing the development of broad, flexible methods that can be applied to diverse problems, and even new, unforeseen applications. As evidence of this trend, an analysis of research output reveals a shift from a diverse set of narrow topics in the early days of binary analysis to the present day, where the majority of investigations pertain to general techniques for processing and understanding software.

This research focuses on a stochastic control problem where the objective function to minimize includes the number of times the process crosses certain thresholds, effectively counting the number of times the process toggles between two states. Unlike traditional barrier methods, our main result shows that if the process is not bounded and the objective function includes the number of state changes, then even in the case of no friction, the value function will not be continuous. To demonstrate this finding, we use a simple example with only two possible states and a underlying stochastic process that can be represented by an array where each element corresponds to the number of times the process crosses a given level within a specified time period.

To explore how leptoquark pairs behave when produced and their subsequent decay in environments with multiple particle collisions, a study creates a comprehensive framework that accounts for both the quark and lepton systems. This analysis, particularly focused on pair production, reveals that leptoquark pairs behave differently due to varying interactions with quarks and lepton systems. Specifically, in collisions that involve proton-proton interactions, a particular combination of leptoquark interactions causes the (T3=1/3, charge=+2e) and (T3=1/3, charge=0) leptoquark pairs to behave differently than the (T3=1/3, charge=+1e) and (T3=1/3, charge=0) pairs. Consequently, this disparity leads to an inequality in the cross-sectional area of the (T3=1/3, charge=+2e) and (T3=1/3, charge=+1e) leptoquark pairs by as much as a factor of twenty-five.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we are showing the potential utility of these lines in certain contexts. With the help of hydrodynamic simulations, we understood the subthermal stimulation of these lines, finding it significant, around 20%, in the coolest molecular gas. This stimulation could either lead to an underestimation of gas temperatures or an overestimation of density, though it is plausible that gas temperatures are lower than calculated. Nevertheless, these lines remain valuable for studying the balance between gas and star formation, as well as the overall metabolism of galaxies, and may also be useful in identifying the gas contributing to submillimeter continuum emission.

Given an arrangement of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, defined by a distance function, and a set of subspaces of the same dimension, there is a problem to determine if there is a linear transformation that represents the arrangement and, using this transformation, calculates the distance between subspaces correctly. This problem is called the series reconstruction problem for arrangements. It is necessary to use a specific distance metric called the Hamming distance, which is based on the number of positions that differ between the binary representations of points. Even though the Hamming distance is a well-known measure, there are challenges in solving the series reconstruction problem for arrangements defined by this distance because it is not possible to calculate the distance between subspaces directly. However, there are ways to estimate this distance, and in this paper, new bounds are established for the number of points in arrangements in $\mathbb{R}^d$ using the Hamming distance. These bounds vary depending on the dimension and include lower and upper limits. In particular cases, such as in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the established upper limit is better than previous records, and in $\mathbb{R}^3$, the established lower limit is better than previous records. Additionally, this paper explores possible relationships between the number of points in arrangements defined by the Hamming distance and well-known sequences like the binomial coefficients or the Fibonacci numbers.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by the gradual decay of elliptical binaries within the Milky Way. Such observations may provide insights into the binaries themselves, as well as informing data analysis techniques for detecting more subtle signals from parallax-distorted sources under the Earth. To advance PTA data analysis, a model has been developed to combine the signals from elliptical binaries with a common mass range (assuming masses above 0.5 solar masses) and various orbital periods. This model enables researchers to test various sky mapping techniques for detecting these signals and to explore the impact of PTA signal detection methods on the recovery of binary properties. It is predicted that PTA experiments will be capable of identifying thousands of elliptical binaries and accurately measuring the masses of neutron star binaries with a precision of up to 0.6 solar masses. The computational expense of searching for these signals is expected to be significant, with an estimated search cost comparable to that required to search for individual-binary signals with similar sensitivity, offering a potential opportunity to streamline searches for a wide range of binary inspirals through the efficient evaluation of a limited set of characteristic templates.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This velocity distribution is observed to remain uniform as the system evolves indefinitely.

Our analysis compares and contrasts various mathematical models being used to study the COVID-19 pandemic, including detailed discussions of epidemic models, asymptomatic infection models, multi-group models, super-spreader events models, travel-related infection models, vaccine evaluation models, and models for predicting healthcare systems' capacity.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple aspects of laser-driven Fermi-Bose atom-molecule conversions, also known as'spinor atom-molecule transformations'. This process is based on the opposition of two out-of-phase coherent populations of atom-molecule condensates, achieved through two-color laser interactions that facilitate three-body recombination. Our research reveals that this process is characterized by both constructive and destructive interferences, influencing the efficiency of recombination and the properties of the resulting atom-molecule pairs. The efficiency of this process is optimized when the two-color laser beams have the same intensity, creating efficient conversions between atom-molecule pairs, as well as efficient isomerization between molecular states, provided that the magnetic coupling between atoms and molecules is minimal. The theoretical predictions presented in this study are compared against experimental data, showcasing the importance of considering both collective effects and magnetic coupling in future implementations.

This research introduces a new technique for efficiently updating the hierarchy of data stored in Semantic Web formats and hierarchies. Previously, updating a hierarchy was shown to be an abstruse problem with no known polynomial-time solution, and was thus deemed an appropriate challenge for sublinear algorithms. Here, we demonstrate that with a large amount of data, a small amount of prior information can be used to assist in finding the hierarchy while keeping the overall computation linear, and with a minimal amount of prior information, the hierarchy can be constructed in a sublinear time. Additionally, we show that updating a hierarchy is equivalent to solving a specific type of integer programming problem, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique using real-world Semantic Web data.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, traditional numerical solutions struggle with speed and are often too cumbersome for real-time use. In contrast, the proposed model leverages the Advection Upstream Splitting Methods (AUSM) scheme and deep learning-based reconstruction techniques to quickly solve the shallow water equations. By utilizing a subset of globally representative data, our model achieves remarkable performance in predicting river flow velocities across various settings. Moreover, we demonstrate the efficacy of our AUSM scheme in real-world river flow violence predictions using a large publicly available dataset. The code for the proposed method has been made publicly available.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a mobile imaging technology that simplifies HDR image creation and fusion for various mobile devices. The proposed system consists of three parts: automatic exposure interval and image fusion techniques have been implemented to streamline HDR photography. The proposed HDR technology enables users to capture high-quality HDR images with a single mobile shot, eliminating the need for multiple exposures. The system's efficiency was tested on a range of scenarios, including both controlled and real-world settings, demonstrating its utility and feasibility.

Causal neural networks, an emerging framework, integrates counterfactual reasoning and neural networks to address counterfactual questions. This report explores the concepts and techniques of causal neural networks by classifying them into three categories: using causal neural networks for counterfactual prediction, incorporating counterfatural information in neural networks, and learning from partial identification. It also delves into the mathematical details of various methods and encourages further exploration of this emerging field.

This note presents a new category of map functions called oriented colored broken submersions, which incorporates map functions that permit a subset of their domain to be smoothly mapped to a submanifold of the target space. We demonstrate that oriented colored broken submersions satisfy the b-principle, a fundamental concept that serves as a fundamental building block in the field of geometric topology. Specifically, it can be used to establish the independence of a particular theorem from a specific set of topological properties of the domain. Moreover, oriented colored broken submersions encompass a broad range of map functions that incorporate map functions that involve multiple iterations of smooth embeddings and a type of map functions called oriented colored submersions. The term oriented colored submersions refers to map functions that can be treated as a combination of orientable surface embeddings with no boundary points. The b-principle is applicable to oriented colored broken submersions, confirming its broad applicability in geometric topology. Notably, this result implies that the Independence Theorem, which states that certain properties of a domain are independent of a specific set of topological properties, can be generalized to include the Mumford conjecture, a well-known geometric topology conjecture, thus providing a solution to a previous open question.

The effectiveness of numerical solutions for cardiac mechanics models depends greatly on the accuracy of their underpinning partial differential equations, but it also relies heavily on the performance of iteration methods and multilevel preconditioners in solving these equations. Research in this area has been driven by the needs of medical imaging techniques such as cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. This paper examines a range of multilevel preconditioners recently proposed for solving cardiac mechanics models, as part of the COMSOlve project. Specifically, it evaluates and compares several preconditioners including local multigrid methods with unusual components such as iterative solvers for stiffness matrices and solvers for mass matrices, and quasi-Newton methods. The study focuses on the performance of these preconditioners across varying iteration sizes, solvers for stiffness matrices, and solvers for mass matrices. It also explores the potential benefits of compact multigrid methods with smaller memory usage and the advantages of quasi-Newton methods. The results are applied to real-world examples involving left ventricle models.

We investigate a unique scenario of random diffusion, driven by a heterogeneous medium whose statistical properties remain unknown, using a model of fractional Brownian motion with specific characteristics. This model can simulate a wide range of scenarios, from highly correlated and anomalous diffusion to unrelated and linear diffusion. The focus is on examining the effects of fractal dimensions of the medium's structure on diffusion patterns. Since the scenario behind the diffusion is randomly changing, we cannot predict the direction of diffusion based on its history. Therefore, this model does not fit the standard definition of anomalous diffusion, which can be distinguished from random diffusion. The term "anomalous diffusion" is used here to describe the behavior of this model, despite its widespread non-linearity. The term "isometric diffusion" is also introduced to describe the model when the fractal dimensions of the medium and the diffusion path are the same. The research shows that even when the statistical properties of the medium are unknown, the fractal dimensions of the structure can be inferred from the diffusion path alone, providing a unique way to estimate the dimensions of a terraine simply by observing the diffusion within it.

A comprehensive theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between optical resonators and waveguides. The proposed framework, which is applicable across various geometries and modes, serves as a foundation for analyzing both individual components and systems made up of multiple resonators and waveguides, including those with Kerr nonlinearity. The method involves utilizing a universal set of coordinates that allows for the easy conversion between different systems and provides unique insights into the behavior of coupled modes. The resulting equations describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear systems and can be solved using a variety of techniques. The developed theory is particularly useful for understanding patterns formed in Kerr nonlinear systems and can be applied to various scenarios, including those with phase singularity and pattern formation in both two-dimensional spaces and waveguides.

A novel method for enhancing the resolution of turbulent velocity patterns has been developed, enabling the direct visualization of vortex dynamics at high Reynolds numbers. The proposed technique, which combines Laplacian-scale-free generative adversarial networks, incorporates an objective function that promotes the maintenance of inherent characteristics of turbulent flows during the upscaling process. By successively applying this method, even extremely small-scale features of velocity fields can be accurately reconstructed. The accuracy of this approach is demonstrated through simulations of turbulent flow with organized vortex structures for both moderate and high Reynolds numbers, as well as the validation of its minimal impact on flow properties such as kinetic energy and enstrophy. The proposed algorithm stands out from more traditional interpolation methods, showing better preservation of intrinsic flow properties and finer-scale dynamics over a wider range of Reynolds numbers. The enhancement of resolution does not depend on specific Reynolds number values, allowing for the direct observation of tiny-scale vortex dynamics and their temporal development without the need for actual simulations at extremely high computational costs.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

Variability management in declarative processes involves accommodating differences in processes that can be further refined, as seen in processes with options, defaults, and exceptions. To handle such processes, a new approach is proposed that combines machine learning and path exploration. The process is represented as a knowledge base with assumptions, and the goal is to identify the necessary process fragments based on input streams, without explicit specification. The approach incorporates a confidence level in the process fragments, which is updated in response to new input, and it prioritizes process fragments for exploration. The approach is demonstrated through experiments using real-world data from a hospital protocol for sepsis treatment.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between algebraic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of varieties.

Determining the factors driving the decline of star-forming galaxies at the edges of galaxy clusters remains an intriguing challenge. To better understand this phenomenon, we examine the link between stellar mass and star-forming activity by analyzing the far-infrared radiation of galaxies. By comparing the distribution of infrared radiation to stellar mass, we find that the shape of this relationship changes above 5 x 10 to the power of 10 suns, becoming less steep than expected. This shift is particularly noticeable when we account for the size of galaxy bulges. By distinguishing between bulge-dominated and disk-dominated galaxies based on their central brightness, we can map the distribution of infrared radiation to stellar mass. Only bulge-dominated galaxies exhibit the reversed slope of the relationship above 5 x 10 to the power of 10 suns. This reversal is likely caused by the shutdown of star formation in these galaxies, which occurs when they migrate to the center of the cluster. The reduced star formation in bulge-dominated galaxies contributes to the decline in star-forming activity at the edges of galaxy clusters.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content in texts from different linguistic backgrounds. Our primary
objective is to classify the sentiment of multilingual text collections.
To achieve this, we developed a convolutional neural network based model and
tested it on a large, publicly available dataset of 9 languages. Our main
finding is that a high overall sentiment classification accuracy of 78% can
be attained. Our model also produces specific language-specific classification
accuracies ranging from 58% for Latin to 88% for Chinese. Our research
invites further exploration into the underlying factors influencing sentiment
classification across different languages.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with diagnostic significance that can be extracted by a combination of technical methods, providing valuable clinical information for accurate treatment choices. Given the limited accuracy of traditional machine learning models in identifying COVID-19 from X-ray images due to their reliance on pre-defined features, a more effective approach involves using artificial neural networks that can automatically extract crucial characteristics from data. Consequently, a framework is proposed to incorporate both machine learning and artificial neural networks to enhance the efficacy of COVID-19 diagnosis based on X-ray images. The proposed framework's ability to extract important characteristics from data is examined, along with the proposed clinical guidelines for intensive care unit admissions in COVID-19 patients. The paper's main contributions are the integration of a novel dataset consisting of X-ray images and medical records, as well as a tailored, multi-task artificial neural network design that can be trained for both image classification and data imputation. Furthermore, clinical ICU admission guidelines for COVID-19 patients are established and evaluated using both leave-one-out and k-fold validation techniques.

The global simplicial bundle functor, which extends the concept of bundle functors to simplicial sets, possesses a unique property: it is a monad that respects simplicial structures. As a result, it generates a simplicial in algebra for any given theory, effectively interpreting bundle functors within the framework of simplicial category. When applied to first-order logic, this results in a simplicial group that represents the bundle functors in the simplicial world.

This paper investigates the issue of erroneous positive relationships in visual relationship detection, which leads to poor performance in frequent relationships. We attribute this problem to the incomplete and misleading information present in confirmed relationship pairs. This COMPLETENESS BIAS hinders the model from focusing on infrequent relationships and inaccurate pairs detracts from the learning process. To address this issue, we develop a novel multi-head sampling strategy to address data incompleteness and a pair-weighting mechanism to address the noise. Implementing these solutions as the COMPLETENESS-AWARE Relationship Detection (CARD) model, we achieve significant performance improvements on popular datasets in relationship detection and on ViOLET in visual language inference.

We've performed simulations of galaxy interactions and collisions and have incorporated the development of bulges through gravitational mergers. Prior research primarily focused on massive galaxies forming bulges as a result of major mergers. Our work highlights the significance of minor and intermediate mass mergers in creating lopsided galaxies, which we believe are prevalent during certain cosmic eras. These mergers, characterized by the accumulation of star-forming material on one side of a galaxy, can contribute substantially to the development of bulges, particularly in low and intermediate mass galaxies. Our model includes the disintegration of small galaxies and star-forming regions that can lead to the formation of dense star clusters and super star clusters. Automatically adjusting the mass resolutions based on the conditions of the cosmic environment, we have observed the formation of massive star clusters and SSCs in the center of galaxies, which we believe were prevalent in very distant galaxies. Our simulated galaxies, which have been formed through collisionless gravitational interactions, exhibit a wide range of shapes, including thick and lopsided bulges that are driven by distributed mass distributions rather than pure mass accretion. This phenomenon is supported by observations of distant galaxies that have been analyzed using Hubble and Spitzer telescopes.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia, Chile, and Mexico have been incorporated into an existing dataset of solar neutron observations. These observations were made on November 7, 2004, following a significant solar flare, and were recorded using hydrogen filled neutron detectors at the CR0, LEO, LWS, HOPETON, HARE, TIEG1, TIEG2, TIEG3, TIEG4, TIEG5, TIEG6, TIEG7, TIEG8, TIEG9, TIEG10, TIEG11, and TIEG12 locations.

This work provides the first haptic simulation evidence that angular momentum added to the surface of a sphere leads to higher spin rates, contrary to lower spin rates found in previous 2D computer simulations. We consider two possible explanations for this discrepancy: the inability to accurately depict the effects of angular momentum in 2D simulations or the unknown influence of planetary ingestion by the star.

True and false news coexist on social media platforms, with false news spreading rapidly due to its interesting and sensational content. While traditional fact-checking methods rely on accurate titles, verifying information requires time and is often subject to bias. To address this issue, we draw on the idea of meta-learning and treat false news emergence as a problem of meta-learning. We develop a novel Multimodal Meta Neural Process Network (MMNPN) to effectively identify false news. MMNPN combines the capabilities of neural process networks and meta-learning, enabling the systematic development of false news-identifying functions through the aggregation of previous experiences. We introduce a new dataset, known as Emergent False News Multimodal Language Inference, which integrates existing datasets by adding video and text modalities, thereby providing a challenging platform for evaluating the performance of MMNPN. We also conduct extensive experiments on this new dataset, demonstrating the superior performance of MMNPN in comparing it to other leading methods.

This research paper examines a periodic conveyance equation, which is a key component of the McKean-Vlasov diffusion process and stochastic logic model. We derive anomalies to the equation's solutions and explore their implications in the context of the original model.

A type of sequence set known as Golay complementary pairs has two pairs of sequences of length 2^m-1, where each pair consists of two identical sequences, and two distinct sequences that are complementary to each other. This research introduces the concept of multi-phase Golay complementary sets, extending the traditional Golay concept to include phase factors. A specific type of bi-phase Golay complementary sets is constructed using matrix decomposition, and a new class of four-phase Golay complementary sets is defined and its construction is outlined. Furthermore, a new method for creating multi-phase Golay complementary sets is proposed by combining two bi-phase Golay complementary sets, and this approach is particularly useful for expanding existing sets to higher phase orders.

Quantum spin transfer via atomic scale processes is a key obstacle for silicon technology, as it hinders efficient switching times in memory applications. To grasp this challenge, researchers need a granular understanding of where and how spin interacts in silicon. This study uses advanced atomic resolution spectroscopy to examine local environments around dangling bonds in silicon. It demonstrates that covalent valleys interact through spin-polarized currents, even when atomic scale processes are considered. Nevertheless, the magnitude of this effect can be altered by bonding atoms, providing a pathway potentially useful for designing valley interactions and controlling spin transfer.

Our investigation focuses on exploring the capability of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in analyzing complex dynamic systems characterized by nonlinear interactions. We demonstrate how GNNs can effectively capture these interactions by applying a convolutional neural network component, which produces useful temporal patterns for a longitudinal study design. Our findings validate the effectiveness of GNNs in modeling such systems and provide valuable insights into the importance of considering nonlinear relationships, time-dependent patterns, and measurement errors in GNN-based modeling. Furthermore, we propose a novel method using GNNs to determine critical parameters that influence a system's dynamics and analyze its advantages in comparison to existing approaches.

We introduce extensions of graded modules and rings in homotopy theory, defining composition operations that incorporate Bockstein connections. These constructions are demonstrated to incorporate combinatorial structures related to permutation groups, thereby establishing connections to discrete mathematics. In particular, our framework yields explicit formulas for counting the number of divisions that arise in homotopy theory, including both even and odd instances.

A cutting-edge medical technology has been developed to assist neurosurgeons in identifying and avoiding critical brain areas during surgical procedures, such as removing tumors. This technology, known as cerebral lesion prediction models, uses advanced mathematical models to analyze patient data and predict areas of damage, but it requires significant training data, a difficult task. A novel approach has been presented, a complex mathematical model called progressive adversarial variational auto-encoder, which can effectively train a model using minimal data, includes a sub-model to recover high-resolution images, and is highly efficient in predicting damage areas during surgical procedures. This model has been successfully applied to real patient data with notable improvements in prediction accuracy.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the compilation process, the GP 2 compiler was upgraded to utilise a more advanced matching algorithm for rooted rules, leading to a significant reduction of compilation time. Additionally, the upgraded compiler is capable of providing valuable insights into program execution, derived from a novel analysis of the relationship between rules and graphs.

This paper presents a novel neural network architecture that incorporates a comparison learning module to enhance feature discrimination and extraction. The proposed network achieves superior performance in comparison to traditional convolutional neural networks, demonstrating enhanced classification capabilities and optimized computational efficiency. The structure's effectiveness is demonstrated through a range of experiments conducted on well-established datasets across various task settings, including image classification, where it shows a notable improvement in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods, and in other tasks where it exhibits comparable performance.

We have discovered an infinite family of finite simple groups whose structure belongs to the star normal quotient type and features a diagonal action on the orbits of 1s, 2s, and a set of three distinguishable 3s within a reliability matrix. This distinction prevents the application of existing classification theories, thereby requiring the development of new computational methods to classify these groups under the star non-quasithin property.

Working with nominal data poses significant challenges, especially when it comes to high-dimensional projections. Despite the importance of incorporating prior knowledge through Group Lasso, its application to nominal data is complicated due to the need to define and estimate the variance of the ratio of the mean of groups to the standard deviation of groups. This estimation issue becomes even more difficult in high-dimensional settings, leading to poor estimation performance and an increased risk of overestimating the model. To address this problem, we propose a new method, ELasso, which bypasses the estimation of this variance ratio by utilizing the U-statistic framework. Although this approach is compatible with a variety of loss functions, we focus on its implementation with the zero-one loss, even though it results in a non-differentiable objective function that complicates optimization. To address this issue, we leverage the iterative shrinkage thresholding algorithm, adapting it to suit our purposes, and implementing an enhanced version of it. Notably, this method offers a significant improvement over the standard Group Lasso for nominal data, outperforming it in terms of estimation performance, model sparsity, and prediction accuracy in various real-world and simulated datasets.

Recent advances in large language models have demonstrated the effectiveness of pretrained foundations for a wide range of applications. Nonetheless, these models have been shown to exhibit biases and inaccuracies when confronted with specialist knowledge, requiring the integration of structured information to achieve satisfactory performance. In response to this challenge, the ABILITY framework has been developed to seamlessly incorporate structured knowledge into large language models. This novel technique enables the effortless integration of specialised knowledge into these models, enabling the selection of integrated models tailored to a particular task or purpose. Furthermore, the ABILITY framework facilitates the retrieval of relevant knowledge from extensive knowledge bases, eliminating the need for manual knowledge curation. This technique has been successfully demonstrated through a set of experiments involving the integration of structured information into models for tasks such as text classification, where the incorporated knowledge is drawn from vast, publicly available knowledge bases like Wikidata.
